title: Steve Jobs on A-players, craftsmanship over process, and taste: Triumph of the Nerds interview (1995)
summary: In a candid 1995 interview, Jobs explains why great products come from content-obsessed teams of A players, not process or ideas alone. He covers the rock tumbler metaphor for teams, why monopolies rot product sensibility, and why taste and a liberal arts background drive computing.

principles.text: Great teams are like a rock tumbler: talented people rubbing against each other polish each other and the ideas.
principles.quote: through that group of incredibly talented people bumping up against each other, having arguments, having fights sometimes, making some noise, and working together, they polish each other.

principles.text: In software the best people are 50-100x better than average, so hold out for A players and never settle for B and C.
principles.quote: I've built a lot of my success off finding these truly gifted people and not settling for B and C players, but really going for the A players.

principles.text: A players recruit A players: a few of them together become self-policing and only want to hire more of the same.
principles.quote: they really like working with each other because they've never had a chance to do that before. And they don't want to work with B and C players.

principles.text: A great idea is not 90% of the work; craftsmanship between idea and product is where the magic lives.
principles.quote: there's just a tremendous amount of craftsmanship in between a great idea and a great product.

principles.text: Process is not content: companies that institutionalize process forget the substance that made them great.
principles.quote: people get very confused that the process is the content. That's ultimately the downfall of IBM.

principles.text: Taste comes from exposing yourself to the best human work and shamelessly bringing it into what you build, with a liberal arts attitude.
principles.quote: it comes down to taste. It comes down to trying to expose yourself to the best things that humans have done. And then try to bring those things in to what you're doing.
